title: Explainer: China eyes overnight rate as main policy tool, what it means for markets
body: The direct market effect is likely to be modest, because the PBOC is formalising a rate it already targets rather than cutting. The market read so far suggests limited impact, with China's 30-year bond yield slipping only about 1 basis point and the overnight rate steady around 1.26%. The bigger question for traders is whether the new anchor is eventually set near today's overnight level of about 1.25%, below the seven-day rate of 1.40%. Markets could treat that as a mild easing signal, which would tend to support Chinese bonds and weigh slightly on the yuan. For the Australian and New Zealand dollars, which often trade as proxies for China, the framework change matters less than whether it comes with genuine easing that lifts Chinese demand. Oil traders will watch the same thing, given China's role as the world's largest crude importer. --- Separately, coming up later today: China LPR preview: rates seen on hold for a 17th month after Q3 GDP beat --- China's central bank wants to steer its economy with the same short-term lever the Fed uses, and while that is not a rate cut, it changes which numbers traders need to watch. Summary: PBOC Governor Pan Gongsheng said on Monday the central bank will study switching its main policy operations from a seven-day tenor to overnight, when the time is right. The overnight reverse repo rate would replace the seven-day reverse repo rate, the main policy rate since 2024, as the central signal for monetary policy.

title: Goldman Sachs sees $25 war risk premium in Brent, forecasts $90 in December and $80 in 2027
body: Goldman's estimate implies Brent is trading well above where supply and demand alone would put it, which leaves prices vulnerable to a sharp drop if the risk of escalation fades, and exposed to further spikes if the conflict widens. The forecast path points lower over time, with the bank expecting a shift into surplus from the fourth quarter to pull prices back toward $80 in 2027, a level consistent with UBS's view that Brent will approach $80 next summer. Near-term support is likely to come from depleted inventories, including a US Strategic Petroleum Reserve at its lowest since 1982, and from investors using oil as a hedge for their stock and bond holdings. For inflation-sensitive markets, a fading premium would ease pressure on central banks and bond yields, while a renewed spike would reinforce the hawkish case. --- Earlier: US strategic oil reserve falls to lowest since 1982 as Iran war release drains stocks --- Goldman Sachs reckons about $25 of every barrel of Brent is a bet on the Iran war getting worse, and if that bet does not pay off, the bank sees prices drifting back toward $80. Summary: Goldman Sachs estimates spot Brent carries a risk premium of nearly $25 a barrel above its fair value, reflecting the risk of supply curtailment and inventory draws if the Iran war escalates. The bank raised its December 2026 Brent forecast to $90 a barrel from $85 and expects an average of $80 in 2027.

title: UBS sees euro recovering to $1.16 by year-end, says slide to $1.11 overshoots fundamentals
body: UBS's view puts the euro's recent weakness down mainly to sentiment rather than fundamentals, which would leave room for a rebound if French budget risks ease. The near removal of pricing for an October Fed hike takes away one of the dollar's main supports, and UBS sees a sustained break below $1.10 as increasingly unlikely as a result. Energy is a key swing factor: the euro area is a large energy importer, so UBS's expectation that Brent will approach $80 by next summer is supportive, while any escalation in the Iran war that lifts oil prices again would weigh on the currency. French bond spreads are the indicator to watch, since narrower spreads would back the recovery case and further widening would undercut it. --- Earlier from analysts at the bank: UBS says neocloud sell-off does not derail AI boom, favours hyperscalers and chipmakers --- UBS thinks the market has sold the euro on worry rather than evidence, and with Fed hike bets fading and a French budget deal in sight, it sees the currency's next move as up. Summary: UBS expects EUR/USD to recover to $1.16 by the end of 2026, after a slide from $1.17 to near $1.11 that it says has gone further than Europe's economy justifies. The bank blames stronger US data, concern over a possible US diesel export ban, rising global bond yields and worries over French public finances. It does not expect a wider European debt crisis and sees a French budget deal as likely, possibly using Article 49.3.

title: UBS says neocloud sell-off does not derail AI boom, favours hyperscalers and chipmakers
body: The UBS view separates two trades that moved together last week: highly leveraged neoclouds, whose models depend on cheap funding, and cash-rich hyperscalers and chipmakers, whose earnings continue to grow. If that distinction takes hold, it could support a rotation within tech rather than a broad exit, with semiconductor names and the large cloud platforms holding up better than specialist GPU renters. The rates backdrop is the key swing factor. With bond yields elevated across developed markets, any further rise in funding costs would weigh most on the neocloud segment. Hyperscaler results over the coming weeks will be the next test, with UBS expecting cloud revenue growth to accelerate. --- The UBS note was before the bounce on Monday, kudos to them! investingLive Americas market news wrap: AI trades rebound but so does oil --- Specialist AI cloud firms are feeling the squeeze from higher rates, but UBS argues that is a funding problem for one corner of the market rather than a crack in AI demand itself. Summary: Shares of neoclouds, specialist providers that rent out AI computing capacity, came under heavy pressure last week on concerns about their growth models as rates stay higher for longer. The sell-off helped drive a weekly fall of about 4.5% in the Nasdaq, its biggest weekly loss since June, with competition from China and revenue worries at AI labs adding to the pressure.

title: Oil Steadies as Traders Monitor Mideast Flows
body: Crude oil prices held firm above $103 per barrel on Tuesday, consolidating recent gains as investors weighed intensifying conflicts in the Middle East and Eastern Europe against evidence of solid supply from the Persian Gulf. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright noted that oil shipments from the Persian Gulf have rebounded to roughly 80% of pre-war volumes, though deliveries of refined products remain constrained. The Trump administration is also authorizing the sale of previously sanctioned oil tankers, allowing them to re-enter the legal crude trade; the global "dark fleet" is estimated to comprise about 1,600 vessels. At the same time, Iran continued to assert control over the Strait of Hormuz, with maritime authorities reporting multiple attacks on commercial vessels. Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen exchanged strikes, while Russia and Ukraine renewed attacks on energy infrastructure. title: Indonesia FDI Rises the Most in Nearly 2 Years
body: Foreign direct investment (FDI) in Indonesia, excluding the financial as well as the oil and gas sectors, jumped 27.5% year-on-year to a record IDR 270.2 trillion (US$14.99 billion) in Q3 2026. This followed a 27.4% increase in Q2 and marked the strongest pace of growth since Q4 2024, despite ongoing global economic uncertainty linked to the conflict in the Middle East. The base metals industry drew the largest share of foreign inflows. By country and territory of origin, Hong Kong was the leading investor, with US$5.2 billion, followed by Singapore (US$5.1 billion), the United States (US$1.7 billion), China (US$1.1 billion), and South Korea (US$0.8 billion). Total direct investment, including both foreign and domestic sources, rose 7.6% year-on-year to IDR 528.7 trillion in Q3 2026, supporting the creation of more than 745,634 jobs. FDI accounted for 51.1% of overall investment during the quarter. The material has been provided by InstaForex Company - www.instaforex.com

title: TSX Slips Despite Softer-Than-Expected Inflation
body: The S&P/TSX Composite Index slipped 0.7% to close at 35,929 on Monday, as investors digested the latest inflation figures and reassessed the outlook for Bank of Canada (BoC) policy. Canada's annual inflation rate accelerated to 3.1% in September, a four-month high, driven largely by higher gasoline prices. While the reading undershot market expectations of 3.2%, it did little to ease concern about the broader inflation trajectory, with policymakers continuing to highlight upside risks to prices. BoC Governor Tiff Macklem said on Saturday that the central bank plans to substantially raise its quarterly inflation forecast this month, reinforcing the hawkish tone he struck last week on energy-related price pressures. Oil prices stayed elevated amid attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, keeping inflation risks front and center for markets. Financials weighed on the index, with major banks broadly weaker: Royal Bank of Canada fell 0.9%, while Bank of Montreal, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, and National Bank of Canada each lost 0.8%. title: Argentina Trade Surplus Widens in September
body: Argentina's trade surplus expanded to $2.98 billion in September 2026, an increase of $2.04 billion compared with the same month in 2025. Exports reached $10.04 billion, up 23.5% year-on-year. All export categories posted higher values than in September 2025, led by fuels and energy, which jumped 89.1%. Exports of manufactured industrial goods rose 17.5%, manufactured agricultural goods increased 16.8%, and primary products grew 9.2%. Imports totaled $7.06 billion, a decline of 1.8% year-on-year. Within the economic-use classification, the sharpest increase was recorded in parts and accessories for capital goods, which rose 11.9%. Imports of passenger vehicles were up 3.5%, while purchases of capital goods fell 10.4% and imports of consumer goods decreased 2.5%. Iran-aligned Houthi militants in Yemen also carried out repeated attacks on Saudi targets last week. Are US Treasuries still a hedge? Citi Australia CEO says the bonds are losing their edge
body: If more investors share Woodruff's view, demand for longer-dated Treasuries as portfolio insurance could weaken, adding upward pressure on the term premium, the extra yield investors demand to hold long-term bonds. That would leave yields more exposed to supply and inflation news. It could also support alternatives that investors have been using as hedges, including commodities. Goldman Sachs has said oil is attracting demand as a portfolio hedge, and it sees central bank buying as structural support for gold. Energy is central to the inflation story: higher oil prices linked to the Iran war helped push the US 10-year yield to its highest since 2007 in September, so any renewed spike in crude would reinforce the case that bonds are a weaker shield. The opposing view, from BlackRock, is that today's higher yields offer more protection than in years. --- A 5% Treasury yield used to be the perfect insurance policy for a stock portfolio, but Citi's Australia chief argues inflation and heavy borrowing have made the policy less reliable, and not everyone on Wall Street agrees. Summary: Citi Australia CEO Mark Woodruff says rising bond supply, persistent inflation and higher neutral interest rates are reducing the appeal of US Treasuries as a portfolio hedge. He said a 5% 10-year yield would usually make Treasuries an ideal hedge for equities, but higher prices and rates have weakened demand.

title: China holds loan prime rates for 17th month as policy focus shifts to short-term rates
body: The hold was widely expected and should have little direct market impact. The more important signals for traders now come from China's short-term rates. Monday's comments from PBOC Governor Pan Gongsheng about moving to an overnight policy rate matter more for the outlook, since the level at which any new rate is set will shape expectations for future easing. With Q3 growth back inside Beijing's target range and the Federal Reserve tightening, the case for imminent cuts is weak, which limits downside pressure on the yuan from rate differentials. For the Australian and New Zealand dollars and for oil, an unchanged LPR offers no fresh stimulus signal for Chinese demand, keeping the focus on fiscal support and incoming activity data. Newswire cut: China kept its one-year loan prime rate at 3.0% and five-year at 3.5%, the 17th straight month on hold. The seven-day reverse repo at 1.40% is the main policy rate, and Pan has flagged a move to an overnight rate, but the LPR still prices most loans. One-line wrap: China's lending benchmarks have not moved in 17 months, and with the central bank now steering through short-term rates, the LPR has become less a policy lever than a price tag on the country's loans. Summary: China left its one-year loan prime rate at 3.0% and its five-year LPR at 3.5% on Tuesday, matching expectations. It is the 17th consecutive month without a change; both rates were last cut in May 2025.

title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6813 – Reuters estimate
body: The fixing mechanism matters most right now because its message has shifted over the past month. For nearly a year, the PBOC has set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, which traders read as an effort to slow the yuan's appreciation, and in late August that gap reached its widest since February, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high. Through September, however, the midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the central bank has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The fixing is still set weaker than models imply, so this looks like a loosening of the brakes rather than their removal. The balance Beijing is weighing is unchanged: a firmer currency supports capital stability and import costs, but too rapid a rise risks eroding export competitiveness while the domestic economy remains soft. The gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest guides to how far the PBOC is willing to let the yuan run.--- The daily fixing is Beijing's quietest but clearest tool for telling markets how fast it wants the yuan to move, and after months of saying slow down, it has lately been saying go, gradually.Summary: The PBOC sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate, or midpoint, at around 0115 GMT, one of the most closely watched signals in Asian FX markets.

title: The Hormuz shipping attacks nobody is counting: inside the US Navy's go-dark guidance
body: Hormuz attack counts are a floor, and a US Navy FAQ may help explain why The official tally of attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz is incomplete, and the body that compiles it says so. In its weekly overview on 16 October, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO) said it was struggling to establish the true number of attacks because the majority of vessels targeted were refusing to report to it. It recorded 12 attacks that week, ten of them inside the Strait, with one vessel lost. It added that it knew of further incidents through other sources but could not include them without verification. For oil traders, that matters more than any single weekly figure. Freight rates, war-risk premium s and assessments of supply risk all lean on these counts. If most attacked ships are staying silent, the published number is a minimum, not a measure. Why ships might stay silent Shipowners have obvious commercial reasons to keep quiet, including insurance complications, exposure with their flag state and sensitivity about routing. But a less noticed document may also be part of the picture. A US Navy FAQ for shipping companies, highlighted in a post on X by the account @angertab, sets out how the Navy supports transits on the southern route through the Strait. It was issued by the Naval Cooperation and Guidance for Shipping (NCAGS) cell at US Naval Forces Central Command (NAVCENT), the unit that liaises with merchant ships.

title: JPMorgan brings JPM Coin to Ethereum mainnet: what changes, and what it means for ETH
body: JPMorgan Chase has extended JPM Coin (ticker JPMD), its US dollar deposit token, to the Ethereum mainnet. Approved institutional clients now have a second public network for moving dollars around the clock. Bloomberg reported the move on Monday, 19 October, citing the bank, and the Ethereum Foundation flagged it the same day. JPMD has run on Base, Coinbase's Ethereum layer-2 network, since November 2025, and Base remains in service. The move is a meaningful step for Ethereum as financial infrastructure. It is not, on current evidence, a new source of demand for ether. JPMD also remains closed to everyone except approved JPMorgan clients. What JPM Coin actually is JPMD is a deposit token: each unit represents one US dollar that a client holds at JPMorgan. That makes it different from a stablecoin such as USDC, which is issued by a non-bank company and backed by reserves held elsewhere. A deposit token is a claim on the bank itself. In effect, it is ordinary commercial bank money moved onto a blockchain. The practical gain is timing. A transfer that would normally wait on banking hours and business-day settlement can complete almost instantly, at any hour, including weekends. Why mainnet, when Base was cheaper Base was promoted on sub-cent fees, and transactions on Ethereum mainnet typically cost more. So the move is not about saving money. Kinexys, JPMorgan's blockchain unit, said it chose Ethereum because so much liquidity and so many tokenized assets already sit there.

title: BlackRock says French bond sell-off is a lesson in selectivity, upgrades US Treasuries
body: BlackRock's view reinforces a theme running through bank research this week: higher yields are now the norm, but the reasons behind them matter more than the level. For euro area bonds, the near-term focus is Moody's decision on France's credit rating, with a downgrade likely to pressure French debt and widen the gap over German Bunds. Any spillover selling in markets such as Spain could prove an opportunity if fundamentals hold up, in BlackRock's view. Its upgrade of US Treasuries signals that the world's largest asset manager sees value in longer-dated US debt at current yields, which could help cap further rises if other investors follow. A rising term premium driven by fiscal worries remains the main risk that could push yields higher still. Elevated energy costs linked to the Iran war add to inflation risks that feed into that premium. --- Higher yields are everywhere, but BlackRock's message is that not all of them are worth having, and France shows the difference between being paid more and being paid enough. Summary: BlackRock says the sharp sell-off in French government bonds shows why investors need to understand what is driving yields higher. France's 10-year yield has risen about 100 basis points since early August to nearly 5%, with a widening spread over German Bunds reflecting fiscal and political risk.

title: Trump holds up Patriot missiles for Ukraine as Russian strikes intensify, officials say
body: The dispute raises the risk of further escalation in a conflict that has increasingly targeted energy infrastructure on both sides, with the clearest risk for oil to the upside. Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and diesel facilities have been a source of supply concern in product markets, and if Washington's pressure on Kyiv to halt them fails, those attacks could intensify, tightening diesel supply further at a time when the Iran war is already keeping crude elevated. A weaker Ukrainian air defence could also leave its own energy system more exposed to Russian strikes. Against that, Friday's US waiver of Russian oil and gas sanctions could ease some supply concerns if it allows more Russian barrels to reach buyers. On balance, the risk skew for oil, and especially diesel, leans higher while the conflict escalates. -- As Russian missiles fall on Kyiv, the interceptors Ukraine needs to stop them are stuck awaiting Washington's sign-off, and the US has not said why. title: Gold Slides for Third Straight Session

The metal also came under pressure from a firmer US dollar and higher bond yields. Oil prices held steady at elevated levels amid ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and Eastern Europe, while Iran continued to assert control over the Strait of Hormuz, a key chokepoint for global energy shipments. In the euro area, the European Central Bank is anticipated to deliver at least one more 25-basis-point hike this year in response to persistent inflationary pressures. title: South Korean Shares Plunge on AI Concerns
body: The benchmark KOSPI tumbled more than 3% to around 5,595 on Tuesday, erasing the previous session's gains as renewed selling in semiconductor shares underscored lingering doubts about the durability of AI-related investment. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix dropped over 3% and 6%, respectively, amid mounting concern that debt-financed AI infrastructure and high borrowing costs are weighing on the sector's outlook. Other major decliners included SK Square (-7.1%), LG Energy Solution (-3.9%), Hyundai Motor (-4.8%), Hanwha Aerospace (-11.3%), Doosan Enerbility (-6.6%), HD Hyundai Heavy Industries (-7.4%), and Kia Corporation (-3.5%). At the same time, South Korea's planned 800 trillion won investment in four semiconductor fabrication plants, along with SK hynix's 2 trillion won supplier financing program, is intended to bolster domestic chipmaking capacity and reinforce the semiconductor supply chain, even as infrastructure constraints and US trade-related challenges persist. title: Australian Dollar Holds Firm
body: The Australian dollar held near $0.70, staying above recent multi‑month lows as investors awaited clearer guidance on the policy outlook. Attention is focused on a speech by RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser on Wednesday, which could shed light on the likelihood of a fifth rate increase this year. Signs have emerged that the labor market may be cooling more quickly than expected, according to a recent RBA comment. Even so, the inflation report due on October 28 remains pivotal for future policy decisions. Core inflation is forecast to rise by 0.9–1.0% in the third quarter, potentially pushing the annual rate to 3.5–3.6%—above both the RBA's 2–3% target band and its current 3.3% projection. On the same day, Governor Michele Bullock and other RBA officials will appear before lawmakers, providing a timely opportunity to discuss the latest data and their implications. Money markets now assign roughly a one‑in‑three probability to a November rate hike, with those odds increasing to about 56% for December. Externally, the Australian dollar also found support from a broadly weaker euro, as mounting political risks in France continued to weigh on the single currency. title: China Holds LPR Rates at Record Lows for 17th Month
body: In October 2026, the People's Bank of China left its key lending rates at record lows for the 17th consecutive month, even as the yuan strengthened on the back of solid economic data that broadly matched expectations. The move underscored policymakers' caution regarding the potential fallout from the Middle East conflict, despite third-quarter GDP growth surpassing forecasts. The one-year loan prime rate (LPR)—the main benchmark for corporate and household borrowing—was held at 3.0%, while the five-year LPR, which guides mortgage lending, remained unchanged at 3.5%. At the same time, industrial production and retail sales posted their fastest growth in six months, and the unemployment rate edged lower. New yuan lending continued to rise in September but stayed below year-earlier levels, as subdued household demand and a broader slowdown in economic activity constrained credit growth. Housing prices also declined further in September; however, the pace of the downturn was the slowest in nine months, helped in part by recent government support measures. title: Japanese Shares Fall on Tech Weakness
body: The Nikkei 225 Index fell 1% to around 64,300 on Tuesday, nearing a one-month low as worries over AI-related investment and rising borrowing costs continued to pressure technology shares. Japanese stocks also lagged Wall Street's overnight rebound—driven largely by US chipmakers—as domestic firms remain especially exposed to AI-driven selloffs. Notable laggards included Kioxia Holdings (-2.9%), SoftBank Group (-4.8%), Taiyo Yuden (-3.4%), Fujikura (-4.2%), and Tokyo Electron (-1.7%). Financials also weakened, with Mitsubishi UFJ down 1.5%, Mizuho Financial off 2.8%, and Sumitomo Mitsui slipping 1.6%. On the policy front, Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda stated that underlying inflation is already approaching the central bank's 2% target, reinforcing expectations of a potentially tighter monetary stance. title: Australian Stocks Retreat from Near 5-Week High
body: Australian shares fell 85 points, or 1%, to 8,760 in early trading on Tuesday, ending a two-session advance as investors locked in profits after the market touched a near five-week high. Sentiment was further weighed by renewed volatility in global technology stocks and growing doubts about the sustainability of AI-related spending. On the domestic front, RBA Assistant Governor Kent remarked that the rise in global neutral interest rates raises questions about whether Australia's monetary policy is sufficiently restrictive, even after four rate hikes this year. His comments cooled confidence in the current policy stance. The broader market decline was partially cushioned by stronger-than-expected Q3 GDP and September activity data out of China, supported by demand during the Golden Week holiday. Sector-wise, technology, logistics, non-energy minerals, and financials led the losses. Heavyweight miners BHP Group (-2.1%) and Rio Tinto (-1.2%) posted sharp declines, while the four major banks slid between 1.5% and 2.7%. Other prominent underperformers included Northern Star Resources (-2.2%), Evolution Mining (-3.1%), and Qantas Airways (-1.7%). Traders are now looking ahead to China's monthly loan prime rate decision, due later today. The material has been provided by InstaForex Company - www.instaforex.com

title: US Futures Edge Higher After Tech Rebound
body: US stock futures inched higher on Tuesday, extending gains after the major indexes started the week on a positive note, buoyed by a rebound in technology shares. Futures linked to the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq 100 each rose at least 0.1%. In Monday's regular session, the S&P 500 climbed 0.41% and the Nasdaq Composite advanced 1.11%, recovering from last week's sharp selloff driven by mounting concerns over AI-related financing. Chipmakers and other mega-cap growth stocks led the rebound: Micron added 3%, Nvidia gained 1.4%, Sandisk jumped 5.5%, Amazon rose 5%, and Tesla increased 3.8%. Investors are now bracing for a busy corporate earnings lineup on Tuesday, with results due from General Electric, Netflix, Raytheon Technologies, United Airlines, General Motors, and others. On the economic front, traders will also be watching data on housing starts and pending home sales for further insight into the health of the US housing market.
